EGY_1970_arm_the_supreme_council: With the civilian facade set aside, authority passes to a council of senior officers meeting behind closed doors in Cairo. The generals present it as a temporary custodianship, a war council for a nation under arms, but the men who sit around the table understand that whoever commands the divisions now commands the Republic. The programme of the army becomes the programme of the state.
EGY_1970_arm_the_generals_cabinet: Portfolios once held by Nasser's political companions are handed to serving and retired generals. Ministries are run like staff sections, with memoranda, deadlines and little patience for debate. Cairo's bureaucrats grumble about barracks manners, but the officers promise that after the humiliation of 1967 only disciplined men can be trusted to deliver results.
EGY_1970_arm_fawzi_or_shazly: The junta is not of one mind. The cautious and methodical war minister, Mohamed Fawzi, believes the nation must be harnessed in its entirety before any new test with Israel. The younger and bolder Saad el-Shazly, hero of the paratroopers, wants a lean professional army and a limited, well-prepared blow. The council must choose whose vision the Republic will follow.
EGY_1970_arm_fawzis_total_mobilisation: Mohamed Fawzi takes the helm and turns Egypt into a single barracks. Reservists are recalled, factories and schools are drawn into the war effort, and the radio speaks of sacrifice and endurance. It is a heavy burden for a poor country, but Fawzi insists that the road back to Sinai runs through every household on the Nile.
EGY_1970_arm_shazlys_professional_army: Saad el-Shazly argues that wars are won by trained specialists, not by crowds in uniform. Under his leadership the army shrinks its ambitions and sharpens its skills, with long drills, realistic exercises and officers promoted on merit rather than connections. Soldiers grumble at the pace, but a leaner force begins to take shape along the canal.
EGY_1970_arm_military_courts: Civilians accused of sabotage, subversion or simply of weakening the national will now stand before officers in uniform. The trials are swift and the verdicts rarely surprising. The generals call it wartime necessity, while lawyers and old judges whisper that the courthouse has become another barracks.
EGY_1970_arm_the_general_intelligence_di: The Mukhabarat is placed firmly in the hands of the army. Its informants fill the cafes of Cairo, its files grow thick with the names of officers, students and journalists, and no rumour is too small to be recorded. The junta sleeps more easily, though few Egyptians do.
EGY_1970_arm_martial_order_in_upper_egyp: Troops and police deploy through the villages of the Said, where feuds, smuggling and the angry sermons of zealous preachers have long defied Cairo. Checkpoints appear on the river roads and village elders are summoned to the garrison. The generals promise order, and the south learns once more how far the capital's arm can reach.
EGY_1970_arm_dissolve_the_party_structur: The Arab Socialist Union, built to give the revolution a mass voice, is stripped of its committees and its pretensions. Local party offices are shuttered or handed to garrison commanders, and the old apparatchiks are retired with polite letters. The officers insist that Egypt needs deeds, not meetings.
EGY_1970_arm_the_barracks_question: Every junta eventually faces the same question. The emergency, it is said, will end with victory or at least with peace, yet the generals have grown accustomed to the Presidential Palace and the offices that come with it. Within the council, quiet arguments begin over whether power should ever be given back.
EGY_1970_arm_civilian_handover: The generals announce that the army's duty is to defend the nation, not govern it. A date is set, parties are invited to draw up platforms, and officers return to their units with their medals and a measure of public goodwill. Many Egyptians doubt it will last, but for the first time in years the ballot box is more than a rumour.
EGY_1970_arm_indefinite_military_rule: The council declares that the emergency has no foreseeable end. Elections are postponed again and again, and the army is proclaimed the permanent guardian of the revolution. The generals grow comfortable in their villas and ministries, and the Republic hardens into a state in which the uniform is the only reliable passport.
EGY_1970_arm_a_field_marshal_president: Abd al-Ghani al-Gamasy, the quiet planner whose maps shaped every Egyptian operation, is elevated to the presidency and the baton of a field marshal. He rules as he planned, carefully, patiently and with an eye for detail. To the public he is a steady hand and to the council a useful figurehead, though few doubt who his real constituency is.
EGY_1970_arm_the_shield_of_the_nation: The army has become more than a service. It feeds its own men, builds the roads, trades abroad and guarantees the borders. Officers speak of a Shield of the Nation, and in schools and barracks alike children learn that the uniform stands between Egypt and its enemies. Whether the shield protects the nation or confines it is left unsaid.
EGY_1970_arm_defense_budget_first: The finance ministry is told bluntly that the army comes first. Bread subsidies and school budgets are trimmed to keep the rearmament on schedule, and civil servants are reminded that the nation cannot eat while the canal is held by the enemy. Few dare to object in public.
EGY_1970_arm_military_factories_for_civi: The armaments works of Helwan and Cairo are ordered to turn their lathes to peaceful use. Refrigerators, pressure cookers and sewing machines roll off lines built for munitions, giving the army a new trade and the public goods that Egyptian shops have long lacked. Critics say the quality is martial, but the shelves are filling.
EGY_1970_arm_army_farms_of_the_western_d: Conscripts with spades are sent beyond the Nile to the oases of the New Valley. Wells are drilled, fields are marked out and the army takes up farming as another form of duty. Officers boast of self-sufficiency, and the desert, for once, seems to answer to the chain of command.
EGY_1970_arm_army_engineers_build_the_ro: The army's engineers, so recently drilled in crossing obstacles, are turned loose on the desert. Ribbons of asphalt reach the oases, the mines and the quarries without a single civilian contractor. It is cheap, fast and remarkably orderly, and every kilometre is a reminder of who is building the nation.
EGY_1970_arm_arms_exports: Egyptian-made rifles, ammunition and spare parts begin to leave the warehouses for Baghdad and the capitals of newly independent Africa. The sales bring in hard currency and friends, and the generals discover that a country that once only bought weapons can also sell them. Western diplomats take careful note.
EGY_1970_arm_military_cooperatives: Officers' clubs, army shops and soldiers' cooperatives spread across the garrison towns, selling food and household goods at prices no private merchant can match. Veterans and their families find a measure of security, and the army gains a loyal following. Small traders watch with mounting unease.
EGY_1970_arm_the_army_economy: Farms, factories, workshops and shops together form a state within the state. The army no longer relies on the treasury alone, and its officers sit on the boards of enterprises that employ thousands. Growth follows, but so does the sense that the economy of Egypt has become the economy of the barracks.
EGY_1970_arm_the_arab_military_pact: Emissaries of the junta travel to Damascus, Baghdad and Amman proposing what Nasser's diplomacy never achieved, a standing military alliance among the confrontation states. Officers speak to officers, bypassing the quarrelling politicians. If the pact holds, the Arab armies may finally act as one.
EGY_1970_arm_arms_from_everyone: Egyptian procurement officers shop wherever the price is right. Soviet tanks, French electronics and whatever else can be had are paid for with cotton, credit and favours, and no single supplier is allowed to hold the army hostage. Moscow frowns, Paris smiles, and the arsenals of Egypt fill steadily.
EGY_1970_arm_the_air_defence_first: The lesson of the War of Attrition is plain, that the Israeli air force rules the sky unless it is made to pay dearly. Missile batteries rise in dense belts along the canal and in the Delta, manned day and night by crews trained with Soviet advisers. The generals are certain that whoever controls the sky controls the crossing.
EGY_1970_arm_the_armoured_fist: Tank crews drill in the desert west of Cairo until the rhythm of manoeuvre becomes second nature. Fresh deliveries of armour are concentrated into formations that can strike with weight and speed once the missile umbrella is spread. The junta wants a fist that is able to hit hard when the moment comes.
EGY_1970_arm_conscription_reform: Service obligations are rewritten so that more men are trained for longer, and exemptions once bought by the well-connected are narrowed. Fathers in the villages complain of lost labour in the fields, but the army insists that a nation which wishes to recover Sinai must be willing to train its sons.
EGY_1970_arm_the_republican_guard_of_the: A trusted corps of picked officers and men is raised to guard the council, the ministries and the broadcasting house. Its soldiers are paid well, fed well and watched closely. The generals no longer fear a coup from the street, only one from within the army itself, and this force is the answer.
EGY_1970_arm_an_army_newspaper: The armed forces journal, once a dry bulletin for the barracks, becomes the voice of the government. Its columns praise the discipline of the soldier, the duty of the citizen and the wisdom of the council. Editors in the civilian press learn to read its tone, and to echo it.
EGY_1970_ye_misr_al_fatat_reborn: The old Young Egypt movement of the thirties returns from the political wilderness, its green banners dusted off and its slogans fitted to a new era. Veterans of the original movement stand beside embittered young officers, united by contempt for the pashas and a hunger for national dignity after the defeat. Egypt, they declare, shall be reborn by its own sons.
EGY_1970_ye_the_mass_rallies: Cairo's squares and Alexandria's seafront fill with columns of marching youth, torches and banners. Speakers promise that the nation will rise as one, and the crowds roar in reply. Whatever the foreign embassies make of it, the government has shown that it can summon the street at will.
EGY_1970_ye_pharaoh_or_crescent: The movement has two souls. One looks to the monuments of Giza and Luxor and sees a proud Egyptian civilisation older than any creed. The other sees the minaret and the faith that has bound the Egyptians for more than a thousand years. The leadership must decide which to place at the heart of its nationalism.
EGY_1970_ye_pharaonic_nationalism: Schoolbooks are rewritten to glorify the builders of the pyramids, and the language of the movement turns to blood and soil along the Nile. Copts and secular intellectuals take heart at being counted as heirs of a common past, while the sheikhs of al-Azhar mutter that the nation is being taught to honour idols of stone.
EGY_1970_ye_islamic_nationalism: The movement embraces the faith as the soul of the nation. Its rallies open with prayers and its programmes speak of a virtuous Egypt, the guardian of Islam and the heart of the Arab world. Ahmed Hussein's later turn toward religion finds a ready audience in the mosques, though not everyone is comfortable with the new tone.
EGY_1970_ye_the_green_shirts: Young men in green shirts drill in school courtyards and on village squares, sworn to the movement and to one another. Their discipline impresses their elders and alarms their opponents. They are the movement's pride, its fist and, some fear, its future police.
EGY_1970_ye_national_youth_service: Every young Egyptian is called to serve, in the fields, in the workshops, in uniform and in the ranks of the movement. The camps teach discipline, literacy and loyalty in equal measure. Parents grumble at the interruption to schooling, but many are proud to see their sons marching with purpose.
EGY_1970_ye_against_the_pashas: The movement turns its fury on the old landed class and the foreign firms that still prosper along the Nile. Palaces are denounced, concessions questioned and cosmopolitan Alexandria is warned that its days of easy indulgence are over. The workers and the poor cheer, while bankers and diplomats count the cost.
EGY_1970_ye_the_piastre_plan: The old Qirsh appeal of 1931 is revived, asking every Egyptian to give a coin toward national industry. Pennies from shopkeepers, students and fellahin are pooled into funds for new Egyptian factories. It is a modest idea, but it gives ordinary people a stake in the nation's machines.
EGY_1970_ye_egyptian_goods_for_egyptians: Shopwindows carry placards urging patriots to buy at home, and foreign wares are taxed and scorned. Small manufacturers and craftsmen, long crushed by imports, find their workshops busy again. Importers complain, and consumers learn that national pride sometimes costs a little more.
EGY_1970_ye_nationalise_the_trade_houses: The great foreign trading houses, whose offices have handled Egypt's cotton and its commerce for generations, are taken over in the name of the nation. London and Paris protest loudly. In Cairo, crowds cheer as the last relics of the capitulations are finally swept away.
EGY_1970_ye_a_national_economy: Egyptian capital, Egyptian labour and Egyptian management now run the commanding heights of the country. The plants hum, the ledgers are kept in Arabic, and the movement can point to a young economy that no longer bows to foreign creditors. Whether it can stand without them remains to be seen.
EGY_1970_ye_the_unity_of_the_nile_valley: Egypt and the Sudan, the movement insists, are one valley and one people, divided only by imperial map-makers. Posters show the Nile flowing unbroken from Khartoum to the sea. In Khartoum this slogan is heard with deep unease, and the Sudanese government wonders where Egyptian ambition will stop.
EGY_1970_ye_against_foreign_bases: The movement tells both Washington and Moscow that Egypt will not be anyone's garrison. Advisers are politely but firmly asked to pack, and the nation is promised independence in fact as well as in name. Egypt's patrons are dismayed, but the street applauds.
EGY_1970_ye_egypt_leads_africa: Egyptian emissaries, teachers and radio broadcasts fan out across the continent, presenting Cairo as the natural leader of a liberated Africa. In Khartoum, Addis Ababa, Chad and Libya the message finds both admirers and wary rulers. The ambition recalls Nasser's, but without the Soviet bargain behind it.
EGY_1970_ye_a_greater_egypt: The dream that began in the cafes of Cairo in the thirties is stated openly, an Egypt reaching beyond the Nile Valley to claim a leading place in the Arab and African world. Soldiers, students and workers march under the same banner, and the leaders speak of destiny. Egypt's neighbours listen with growing alarm.
EGY_1970_ye_the_youth_army: Boys barely out of school are formed into battalions under the green banner, trained by veterans who still remember the previous war. They are loud, enthusiastic and eager, and the regular officers watch with a mixture of fascination and misgiving. Their passion is plain, and their discipline is yet to be proved.
EGY_1970_ye_the_leaders_succession: The founder is ageing and the movement must face what comes next. Rival lieutenants court the youth, the officers and the old guard, each insisting that they alone carry the true flame. Behind the cheering crowds, the question of succession quietly decides everything.
EGY_1970_ye_a_movement_state: The movement and the state become one. Party cells appear in every ministry, every factory and every classroom, and loyalty to the cause is the surest path to promotion. The leaders speak of national unity, and dissenters learn that there is no room for opposition within a revolution.
EGY_1970_ye_a_national_republic: The movement chooses to give its nationalism a constitutional form. A republic is declared with elected institutions, a national assembly and a president who answers to the voters. The old militants are uneasy at the compromise, but the public welcomes a state that appears to belong to everyone.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_new_council: A new Revolutionary Command Council is sworn in, made up of younger and angrier officers who regard Nasser's heirs as tired and compromised. They speak of finishing the revolution that began in 1952 and of purging all who have grown fat on it. The old order in Cairo has reason to be afraid.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_colonels_proclamation: On the radio, a colonel reads out the council's proclamation. The old regime is condemned, the war will be fought without compromise, and every Egyptian is summoned to serve. The tone is blunt and the promises are large. In the barracks the junior officers cheer, and in the ministries clerks quietly clear their desks.
EGY_1970_rcc_purity_or_technocracy: The council cannot agree on what kind of revolution it is making. One faction demands ideological purity, with the faithful rewarded and the doubtful removed. Another argues that only competent engineers and planners can rebuild the nation. The choice will shape the character of the new regime.
EGY_1970_rcc_revolutionary_purity: Loyalty becomes the measure of every man. Committees review the record of officers, officials and teachers, and those with doubtful pasts are removed. The faithful are honoured, and the creed of the revolution is recited in every school. The council grows ever more suspicious of anyone who thinks for himself.
EGY_1970_rcc_technocratic_militarism: Engineers in uniform are placed in charge of ministries, factories and research institutes. The council trusts the slide rule over the slogan, and the results are measured in tonnes, kilowatts and schedules. Ideologues sulk at the sidelines while the army's technicians quietly remake the state.
EGY_1970_rcc_revolutionary_tribunals: Special tribunals are set up to try speculators, saboteurs and corrupt officials. Proceedings are rapid and public, and the sentences are severe. The poor cheer when a notorious profiteer is led away, and the rich begin to wonder whose turn is next.
EGY_1970_rcc_militarise_society: Every institution takes on a martial tone. Students march, workers drill and civil servants wear uniforms on state occasions. Whole neighbourhoods are organised into units with commanders, and Egypt begins to look like a country preparing for a war that is always about to begin.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_revolutionary_economic_: A new body of officers and planners is given authority to override ministers, banks and managers. Orders are issued in the name of the revolution, and projects that once languished in committee are suddenly begun. The economy is to be run like a campaign.
EGY_1970_rcc_confiscate_the_new_class: The council denounces a new class of contractors, importers and senior officials who have grown rich during the years of defeat. Villas are seized, bank accounts are frozen and the proceeds are poured into the national treasury. The crowds approve, while the middle class lies awake wondering about their own savings.
EGY_1970_rcc_labour_battalions: Workers are enrolled into disciplined battalions and sent wherever the nation needs them, to docks, building sites and canal works. They are fed, housed and paid, and they are not free to leave. Foremen are replaced by officers, and the trade unions learn to call their members comrades-in-arms.
EGY_1970_rcc_a_command_economy: Prices, wages, quotas and investment are decided in the council's planning rooms. Directors of factories receive orders rather than advice, and the market is treated as an enemy to be starved. Output rises and shortages fall, but the clerks of the plan hold more power than the people they serve.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_canal_bunker_line: Along the western bank of the canal, concrete casemates and sand ramparts rise under the desert sun, a chain of fortified positions meant to hold the line whatever the cost. Gunners and sappers work day and night under the eyes of enemy aircraft. The council is determined that no Israeli column will cross.
EGY_1970_rcc_a_revolutionary_foreign_pol: Egypt declares itself the vanguard of the Arab revolution and begins to export it. Agents and broadcasts reach into Libya, the Sudan and Syria in support of like-minded officers, while Washington is denounced in every speech. Friends are few, but the council values loyalty over comfort.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_iron_republic: The revolution is finished, or so its architects claim. A state of order, discipline and steel stands where the monarchy and the old parties once did. Citizens salute the flag, heed the radio and expect nothing else. For the council the Iron Republic is the proof that the sacrifices were justified.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_national_guard: A paramilitary guard is raised from the most loyal workers, students and veterans, issued with rifles and sent to patrol the factories and the streets. It stands apart from the regular army, answers only to the council and reminds the generals that they too can be watched.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_shock_divisions: Picked soldiers are gathered into formations trained for ruthless offence, with the best armour and the youngest, hardest officers. Their motto is attack and their schedule leaves no room for doubt. The council sees in them the spearhead that will smash the enemy's line when the day arrives.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_state_security_courts: A permanent system of security courts takes over from the improvised tribunals. It has its own prosecutors, its own prisons and its own rules, all in the name of protecting the revolution. The police gain confidence, and the lawyers learn how little their briefs now matter.
EGY_1970_rcc_autarky_of_the_nile: Egypt is told to rely on nothing but itself. Imports are curbed, foreign advisers are sent home and every household is urged to make do. Sanctions and embargoes hold little terror for a state that has decided to stand alone. The sacrifice is real, but so is the pride.
EGY_1970_rcc_the_council_divides: As victory over its enemies draws near, the council turns on itself. Rival officers accumulate supporters, ministries become fiefdoms and whispers of conspiracy fill the corridors. Everyone realises that the revolution cannot have two heads for long, and that the next decision of the council will determine who survives it.
EGY_1970_rcc_a_single_leader: One colonel emerges from the quarrels, and the others fall in behind him or fall silent. He becomes the voice of the revolution and the sole interpreter of its will. His portrait appears on every wall, and the council becomes his audience.
EGY_1970_rcc_collective_command: The officers agree to rule together, with decisions taken by the council and no single man placed above it. It is a fragile balance of rivals who trust each other only so far, but it spares the Republic the folly of a lone ruler. In the corridors of power, argument is kept alive.
EGY_1970_mon_the_return_of_the_king: After eighteen years in exile, the former king returns to Egypt. Fuad II, who was only a child when the Free Officers sent his family away, steps onto the quay at Alexandria to the sound of cannon and cheering crowds. For some, it is a restoration of lost dignity and for others a humiliating step back in time.
EGY_1970_mon_the_royal_council: A council of elder statesmen, loyal officers and men of the old court is gathered around the throne. Surviving ministers of the monarchy, landowners and veteran diplomats advise the young king in whispers. They bring experience and nostalgia in equal measure, and the republic's critics are quick to say that the pashas are back.
EGY_1970_mon_constitution_or_prerogative: The restored monarchy must decide what kind of king Egypt will have. One camp points to the constitution of 1923 and argues that the crown will survive only if it rules with parliament. The other holds that after the chaos of the republic, the people need a ruler with real power. The palace is divided.
EGY_1970_mon_a_constitutional_monarchy: The king swears to uphold the constitution, and the doors of parliament are opened once more. Parties are permitted, newspapers print freely and the crown presides above the quarrels of politicians. London and the Western capitals are delighted, though the veterans of the old palace camarilla sigh at the loss of authority.
EGY_1970_mon_the_royal_prerogative: The crown retains the right to appoint ministers, dissolve assemblies and decide matters of war and peace. Parliament may talk, but the king will decide. The royal court speaks of order and continuity, and the liberal press is told to remember how the last parliamentary age ended.
EGY_1970_mon_the_parliament_of_the_kingd: Deputies file into the chamber for the first time in a generation. The veterans of the New Wafd appear in dark suits, proud and a little surprised to be back in the game. Whatever the limits placed on it, the Parliament of the Kingdom gives the new order a voice and an air of legitimacy.
EGY_1970_mon_the_royal_guard: Handpicked soldiers, resplendent in ceremonial uniforms but armed with modern weapons, are charged with defending the king and his palace. Their loyalty is to the person of the monarch rather than to any general or party. The army's officers watch with mixed feelings.
EGY_1970_mon_abdeen_palace_restored: The great palace in the heart of Cairo, long a museum and a ministry, is cleaned, regilded and returned to the crown. Chandeliers are rehung and the old ceremonies revived. The great landowners return to court, delighted to see the world they knew restored, while the fellahin ask what it means for them.
EGY_1970_mon_return_the_royal_estates: Lands taken from the royal family in 1952 are returned to the crown, together with the revenues that come with them. The estates are a visible sign of the king's rehabilitation, and a pointed reminder to the peasants who farmed them of how much has changed.
EGY_1970_mon_the_royal_cotton_company: A new company under royal patronage takes up the management of Egypt's most famous export. Long-staple cotton again flows from the Delta through Alexandria's brokers to the mills of Lancashire and beyond. Buyers recall the golden days of the trade, and for the first time in years the ledgers are optimistic.
EGY_1970_mon_the_crown_development_fund: The king writes to his fellow monarchs of Arabia and the Gulf, inviting them to place their wealth in the rebuilding of Egypt. A fund bearing the crown's name is to channel their money into canals, ports and housing. It is a bold appeal from one throne to others, and the response will show how much loyalty the royal name still commands.
EGY_1970_mon_an_investors_kingdom: Egypt is presented to the world as a stable, hospitable kingdom where capital is welcome and property is secure. Bankers from Beirut, Kuwait and London visit the offices of the new ministry, and the old arguments against foreign money are put aside. The crown's reputation is the guarantee.
EGY_1970_mon_royal_irrigation_board: A board of engineers, old hands from the days of the monarchy and young graduates, is charged with the canals, barrages and pumping stations of the Nile Valley. The king's name is attached to every new channel, and the fellahin find that water arrives more reliably than it has for years.
EGY_1970_mon_tourism_of_kings_and_pharao: The monarchy discovers an unexpected asset in its heritage. Visitors come to see the pyramids and Luxor, but also the palaces, the royal train and the old courts of Cairo. Hotels reopen, guides polish their English and French, and the restored crown helps to make Egypt fashionable again.
EGY_1970_mon_a_royal_economy: Cotton, tourism, Gulf investment and the improved channels of the Nile together give the kingdom something it has lacked for years, a sense of economic confidence. The treasury is healthier, merchants return and the court proudly attributes it all to the wisdom of the crown.
EGY_1970_mon_the_brotherhood_of_crowns: Fuad II is received with honours by the kings of Arabia, Jordan, Morocco and the Shah of Iran. The old rivalries are put aside, and the monarchs pledge to stand together against revolution wherever it breaks out. For Egypt, so recently the home of the Arab revolution, the change of company is remarkable.
EGY_1970_mon_friends_in_london: The old connection with Britain, once a source of resentment, is quietly revived. Ministers visit Whitehall and British firms return to the Nile. Egypt's merchants hope for easier trade and the court for the dignified friendship of a fellow crown.
EGY_1970_mon_the_shahs_friendship: Fuad II's family connection to the Pahlavis, linked by marriage in the previous generation, becomes the basis of a political understanding. The Shah, who wishes to see monarchy defended from Cairo to Tehran, offers the friendship of a rich and ambitious neighbour. A bond between two thrones is a new feature of Middle Eastern politics.
EGY_1970_mon_king_of_egypt_and_the_sudan: The court revives the old title worn by the grandfather and speaks once more of the unity of the Nile Valley under the crown. The palace is restored, the economy is sound, friends abroad are secured and the succession is settled. Loyalists believe that the dynasty has come home for good, while Khartoum watches with trepidation.
EGY_1970_mon_the_royal_army: The army is given a royal character, with new colours, new regimental names and honorary colonels from the court. Officers who had assumed that the monarchy would fear them discover that it intends to rely on them. Their loyalty is bought with pride and with tanks.
EGY_1970_mon_the_crown_prince: The question of who will carry the crown into the next generation turns to the education of the heir. Tutors, officers and clerics compete to shape the young prince, and the palace argues about whether he should be groomed for ceremony or for command. In a monarchy, the nursery is also a political arena.
EGY_1970_mon_a_regency_council: The king agrees to share his authority with a council of trusted advisers. The ministers, the generals and the elder statesmen of the court will govern in his name until the heir is ready. The arrangement is dignified and steady, and spares the crown from risking everything on one man.
EGY_1970_mon_the_king_rules: The king takes the reins of government himself. Ministers become servants of the crown, and there is no intermediary between the throne and the people. Supporters hail a strong monarch for hard times, while the old parliamentarians recall the lessons of the previous reign with a shudder.
EGY_1970_the_economy_of_the_front: Since 1967 Egypt has lived on a war footing. The canal is closed, tourism has dried up and a large part of the national income goes to the army. Ministers speak of the economy of the front, in which every factory, field and workshop is judged by its contribution to the eventual reckoning with Israel.
EGY_1970_austerity_for_the_front: Egyptians are asked to tighten their belts. Imports of luxuries are curbed, bread and tea remain, and radio announcers urge patience until the day of liberation. Housewives queue and shopkeepers grumble, but most accept that a nation at war cannot expect comfort.
EGY_1970_which_way_for_the_economy: The post-Naksa economy is at a crossroads. Years of state planning have built factories and schools but also queues and bureaucracy. Some voices demand a deeper commitment to Arab socialism, others call for opening the doors to foreign capital, and still others for an economy built on Islamic principles. The choice will define the Egypt of the coming decade.
EGY_1970_deepen_arab_socialism: The state remains the engine of development. Factories, banks and great estates stay in public hands, and the unions are promised a larger voice. The philosophy of Nasser is not abandoned but extended, with the conviction that Egypt's workers and fellahin will win their prosperity through planning rather than the market.
EGY_1970_infitah: Egypt throws open its doors. Foreign investors, Gulf financiers and importers are welcomed, and the state steps back from the markets it once commanded. New hotels and shopping arcades appear in Cairo, a few fortunes are made quickly, and workers and clerks wonder who will pay for the prosperity.
EGY_1970_the_islamic_economy: Economic life is to be ordered according to the principles of the faith. Interest is condemned, charity is organised and trade is conducted in accordance with the law of Islam. The scholars of al-Azhar bless the project, and the economists of the ministries labour to translate old principles into modern accounts.
EGY_1970_public_sector_holdings: The state's factories, mills and trading firms are grouped into great holding companies under the guidance of the planners. Directors answer to ministers and ministers to the Presidency. The public sector is large, proud and not always efficient, but it is the foundation of the socialist order.
EGY_1970_ration_cards_and_price_controls: Every family receives a ration card entitling it to rice, sugar, oil and bread at fixed prices. Inspectors patrol the markets to enforce the ceilings. It is a cumbersome system, but it guarantees that the poor will not starve, and it binds the people to the state that feeds them.
EGY_1970_soviet_credit_lines: Moscow extends long-term credit for machinery, weapons and development projects, to be repaid in cotton, rice and a share of Egyptian output. The arrangement keeps the economy afloat but ties it ever more closely to the Soviet Union. Egyptian officials visit Moscow's ministries as supplicants and as partners.
EGY_1970_free_zones: At Port Said and Suez, customs barriers are lowered and foreign firms are invited to set up warehouses, assembly plants and banks. Cranes, container yards and bonded storage promise to turn the damaged canal cities into trading hubs. Local people hope for work, and nationalists fear for sovereignty.
EGY_1970_the_gulf_investment_wave: Delegations from Kuwait, Riyadh and the Emirates arrive in Cairo with large sums and large ambitions. They are offered contracts for housing, agriculture and tourism, and they are treated as honoured guests. For the first time, the oil wealth of the Gulf flows west to the Nile.
EGY_1970_cut_the_subsidies: The government reduces the subsidies on bread, fuel and basic goods, arguing that the treasury can no longer carry them. Economists applaud, but the poorest quarters of Cairo and Alexandria are filled with anger. The reform is necessary, and nobody can say whether the people will accept it quietly.
EGY_1970_islamic_banks_and_sukuk: The first Islamic banks open their doors in Cairo, offering profit-sharing accounts and trade finance without interest. Pious savers, who had long kept their money under mattresses, bring it into the system. Bankers from the Gulf look on with approval and a little curiosity.
EGY_1970_tourism_reopened: Visitors return to Egypt's temples, tombs and beaches. Guides reappear at the pyramids, hotels repaint their lobbies and tour operators advertise the Nile once more. Tourism brings foreign currency and also work for thousands, from camel drivers to chambermaids.
EGY_1970_central_bank_reform: The central bank, long a department of the treasury, is given real authority over credit, currency and the banking system. Its economists, trained in London and Washington, bring order to the books and discipline to monetary policy. Inflation is a persistent enemy, and the new governor regards it as such.
EGY_1970_an_egyptian_economic_model: After years of improvisation, Egypt arrives at an approach all its own, neither a copy of Moscow nor a transplant from the West. Economists call it the Egyptian model, adapted to the Nile and its people. Whether socialist, open or devout in character, it is homegrown, and that makes it durable.
EGY_1970_the_high_dam_completed: At Aswan, the great dam that Nasser staked his reputation upon is complete. Lake Nasser stretches far into Nubia, the Nile is tamed, and floods and droughts become memories. Soviet engineers and Egyptian labourers take a justified pride, and the Republic has a monument that can be seen from the stars.
EGY_1970_electrify_the_villages: Power lines run from Aswan along the Nile and into the villages that have known only oil lamps. Electric light appears in the evenings, pumps and mills begin to turn, and a radio is soon in every coffeehouse. The fellahin begin to believe that the revolution has something for them.
EGY_1970_lake_nasser_fisheries: The vast new lake is stocked with fish, and fishing cooperatives spring up along its shores. Boats and nets appear on the water where villages once stood, and a new industry takes hold in the shadow of the dam. Fish from Nasser's lake begin to appear on dinner tables across Egypt.
EGY_1970_silt_and_salt: The dam brings an unwelcome side. The annual flood that carried fertile silt to the fields is gone, farmers are forced to buy fertiliser, and salt begins to creep into the soil. The Delta coast is eroding and the water table is rising. The gift of the dam must be paid for, and Egypt must now choose how.
EGY_1970_the_fertiliser_industry: Plants at Aswan and in the Delta turn out artificial fertiliser to replace the vanished silt. Villages that once relied on the flood now depend on sacks from the state cooperative. Yields rise, and so does the dependence of the fellah on the factories of the Republic.
EGY_1970_tile_drainage_programme: Engineers set to work laying thousands of kilometres of clay and plastic pipe beneath the fields. The pipes carry off the salty water and keep the roots dry. It is slow, dull and expensive work, but it keeps the soil alive, and the cultivators of the Delta are grateful.
EGY_1970_the_agricultural_cooperatives: Villages are organised into cooperatives that share seed, credit, machinery and marketing. Small farmers, once at the mercy of money-lenders and landlords, now sit on the boards of their own societies. The state takes its share, but the peasant at last has a voice, if not always a vote.
EGY_1970_cotton_is_king: The white gold of the Nile again takes pride of place. Fields are devoted to long-staple cotton, which earns the foreign currency needed for machinery and arms. The mills of Mahalla and the brokers of Alexandria prosper, though the cultivators ask what they will eat.
EGY_1970_bread_before_cotton: Land is turned over from cotton to wheat, maize and beans. The government decides that a nation which cannot feed itself cannot be independent. Export earnings suffer, but the bread queues grow shorter, and the planners are content that Egypt's fields should serve Egypt's stomachs first.
EGY_1970_reclaim_the_desert: Pumps and canals push the green back into the desert. New villages rise in the western oases and along the margin of the Valley, settled by young graduates and families from the crowded Delta. It is a gamble against sand and salt, but the dream of a second Egypt is hard to resist.
EGY_1970_family_planning: Clinics, posters and radio campaigns urge Egyptians to have fewer children. Nurses visit villages with advice and supplies, and the government speaks of quality over quantity. The sheikhs object, and many families hesitate, but the planners know that no dam can feed an endless multiplication of mouths.
EGY_1970_the_strength_of_numbers: Egypt's millions are a strength, not a burden, declares the government. Large families are honoured, and the growing population is described as the nation's wealth in labour and in soldiers. Planners worry about housing and bread, but the leadership prefers to count the future conscripts.
EGY_1970_the_gift_of_the_nile: The ancient saying that Egypt is the gift of the Nile is made true again in the age of the dam. Water, power, fertiliser and cultivation work in concert, and the fields of the Valley and the desert alike yield harvests that earlier generations could not imagine. The Nile has been mastered, not merely endured.
EGY_1970_industrialise_egypt: The great promise of the revolution was that Egypt would be a land of factories as well as of fields. Even in wartime the ministries of industry return to their blueprints, believing that an economy built on cotton alone will always be at the mercy of others. The path to strength runs through the foundry and the mill.
EGY_1970_helwan_steel: At Helwan, south of Cairo, the blast furnaces and rolling mills are expanded. Soviet technicians and Egyptian engineers work shoulder to shoulder to increase the output of the iron and steel works, the backbone of a modern industrial nation. Every ingot is a small answer to those who said Egypt could never build.
EGY_1970_nag_hammadi_aluminium: With electricity flowing from the High Dam, Upper Egypt can at last support heavy industry. At Nag Hammadi, a smelter is raised to turn imported ore into aluminium for cables, vehicles and aircraft. The sleepy town in the Said finds itself part of the industrial age.
EGY_1970_el_nasr_automotive: The El Nasr factories at Helwan assemble trucks, buses and cars under Egyptian management. Workers who once repaired imported vehicles now build their own, and though the models are modest, the symbolism is not. Cairo's streets are beginning to fill with machines made in Egypt.
EGY_1970_mahalla_textiles: At Mahalla al-Kubra, the great textile mills spin and weave the cotton of the Delta into cloth for the nation and for export. Tens of thousands of workers have found a living there, and their strong solidarity makes them a force the government does well to heed. The mills give Egypt both its wardrobe and its working class.
EGY_1970_oil_of_the_gulf_of_suez: Under the waters of the Gulf of Suez lies a promising treasure. Rigs rise at fields such as El Morgan and Ramadan, and foreign and Egyptian companies drill along the coast. For a country long short of foreign currency, the prospect of becoming an oil exporter is intoxicating.
EGY_1970_the_sumed_pipeline: A pipeline from the Red Sea coast to the Mediterranean is proposed to carry Gulf crude around the closed canal. With Arab capital and Egyptian land, the project promises to turn the loss of the canal into an opportunity. Pumping stations and tank farms begin to appear along the desert route.
EGY_1970_abu_qir_gas: Natural gas discovered off the coast near Alexandria fuels the thermal plants of the Delta. Pipelines carry it ashore at Abu Qir, and furnaces and fertiliser works begin to burn the new fuel. Egypt's engineers are pleased to find that the sea holds more than fish.
EGY_1970_the_el_dabaa_reactor: On the Mediterranean coast at El-Dabaa, the long-discussed nuclear power station finally rises from the sand. Egyptian scientists speak of electricity and progress. In Tel Aviv and in Western capitals, the same word is heard with suspicion. Egypt has joined the atomic age.
EGY_1970_thermal_power_for_the_delta: Conventional power stations burning oil and gas are built at Cairo and Alexandria, quick to construct and well understood. Their chimneys provide the electricity that the factories of the Delta need, without the controversy of the atom. Engineers call it sensible and nationalists call it timid.
EGY_1970_rebuild_the_railways: The railways laid by British engineers have suffered from war and neglect. Track is relaid, locomotives are overhauled and stations are repainted, and the trains once again run along the Valley. For a poor country, the railway remains the surest way to move people and goods.
EGY_1970_the_cairo_metro: Beneath the crowded streets of Cairo, tunnels are driven for an underground railway. The congested capital, long choked by trams, buses and donkey carts, will gain a modern artery. Engineers fear the groundwater and the antiquities, and the city's commuters pray for success.
EGY_1970_the_desert_roads: Asphalt roads stretch across the desert to the oases, the Red Sea and the mines of the south. Lorries now cross in hours distances that once took days by caravan. The roads bind the far corners of the Republic to the capital and bring the desert within reach of the plan.
EGY_1970_industrial_heartland: Smelters, mills, refineries and assembly lines are linked by new roads, rails and cables. Visitors from Africa and the Arab lands come to Egypt to see how an Arab nation can make steel, aluminium and cars. Cairo's planners proudly speak of the industrial heartland of the Arab world.
EGY_1970_rebuild_the_armed_forces: The Six Day War left the Egyptian army broken, its equipment lost in the Sinai and its pride in ruins. In the years since, a new force has been quietly reassembled under Soviet instruction. Officers now speak of rebuilding from the ground up, in order to fight again, and to win.
EGY_1970_end_the_amer_clique: The favouritism that placed friends of Field Marshal Amer in command of divisions he never understood is rooted out. Officers are promoted on competence, not loyalty, and the chiefs of the humiliated army are replaced by younger professionals. The purge is painful, but few mourn the old order.
EGY_1970_the_educated_conscript: Egypt's schools and universities now supply a new kind of soldier, a high-school or university graduate able to read a technical manual and operate a modern weapon. Graduates in uniform serve for long years, and the army learns to rely on brains as well as on numbers.
EGY_1970_infantry_against_armour: Israeli armour terrified the Egyptian infantry in 1967. Now, small teams equipped with Sagger wire-guided missiles and RPG-7 launchers are trained to meet the tanks head on. The soldiers practise until the drill is automatic, and confidence slowly takes the place of dread.
EGY_1970_the_armoured_divisions: The tank divisions, savaged in the Sinai, are rebuilt with fresh Soviet armour. Crews train to fight as coordinated formations rather than as scattered columns. The army's commanders have studied the lessons of the previous war closely, and they intend to apply them.
EGY_1970_the_bridging_engineers: Engineers rehearse the greatest obstacle of all, the crossing of the Suez Canal and the breaching of the sand ramparts beyond it. Pontoons, bridging equipment and powerful water cannons are tested on mock canals in the desert. The success of any offensive may depend on these quiet, unglamorous men.
EGY_1970_soviet_deep_battle: Soviet advisers push for an Egyptian army trained in the manner of the Red Army, with mass, depth and the relentless advance of successive echelons. Staff officers learn the doctrine in Moscow's academies and in Egyptian field exercises. It is powerful, orthodox and closely tied to Soviet supply.
EGY_1970_an_egyptian_doctrine: Egyptian planners conclude that they cannot match Israel in the air or in manoeuvre, and decide to fight on their own terms. A limited offensive under an umbrella of missiles, seizing a strip of the east bank and holding it, will be the foundation of their plans. The doctrine is realistic, defensive and distinctly Egyptian.
EGY_1970_western_training: Egyptian officers attend courses in Western staff colleges and study the methods of NATO armies. Instructors from abroad teach flexibility, initiative and the use of combined arms. The change worries Moscow and intrigues Washington, and a few veterans mutter that it is un-Egyptian.
EGY_1970_al_saiqa_commandos: Elite units trained for raids behind enemy lines are expanded under the name of the Sa'iqa. They cross the canal at night, ambush patrols and strike at outposts, proving that Egyptian soldiers can fight on equal terms. Their exploits are celebrated on the radio and envied in the regular ranks.
EGY_1970_the_republican_guard: The guard formed to protect the President and the institutions of the Republic is built into a trusted and well-equipped corps. Its officers are chosen for loyalty as much as skill, and in a land that has seen coups before, its presence is reassuring to some and ominous to others.
EGY_1970_the_air_defence_command: The air defence forces become a separate service, with their own command, their own academy and their own prestige. Missile batteries and radar stations are knitted into a network, and crews practise relocating, camouflaging and hiding. Israel's pilots, who once flew with impunity, begin to meet resistance.
EGY_1970_rebuild_the_air_force: On 5 June 1967 the Egyptian air force was destroyed on the ground. Now new MiGs arrive in crates from the Soviet Union and fresh pilots are trained to fly them. The commanders vow that never again will the sky be lost in the first morning of a war.
EGY_1970_hardened_shelters: Concrete shelters, built to withstand bombs, now cover the aircraft of the Egyptian air force. Runways have been dispersed and repair crews drilled to fix them in hours. The lesson of the first morning of June 1967 has been learnt in concrete and steel.
EGY_1970_pilot_training_at_bilbeis: At Bilbeis, young cadets are put through a demanding course of instruction. Instructors, both Egyptian and Soviet, teach them to fly, navigate and fight. The programme turns out a generation of pilots who will carry the reputation of the air force into the next war.
EGY_1970_missile_boats: In October 1967, small Egyptian missile boats sank the destroyer Eilat, the first ship in history to be sunk by missiles in this way. The navy has taken the lesson to heart. A growing flotilla of fast, heavily armed craft now guards Alexandria and Port Said, and the sailors are proud of their small ships.
EGY_1970_blockade_bab_el_mandeb: Egypt's navy looks beyond the Mediterranean and eyes the narrow strait that guards the southern Red Sea. If Israeli shipping can be stopped at Bab el-Mandeb, the enemy's access to the Indian Ocean will be cut and the strangulation of Eilat will begin. Ships, mines and submarines are readied for the task.
EGY_1970_the_military_factories: Egypt cannot rely on foreign suppliers forever. The ordnance works of Cairo and Helwan are expanded to make ammunition, small arms and spare parts, and the army's technical corps trains a workforce in the arts of industrial production. A nation that makes its own munitions is harder to bring to its knees.
EGY_1970_the_helwan_aircraft_works: The supersonic HA-300 project, abandoned in 1969, is brought back from the archives. German engineers are gone, but Egyptian and foreign experts pick up the work at Helwan. Nasser's old dream of a national fighter aircraft lives again, and even partial success would be a source of great pride.
EGY_1970_the_missile_programme: Egyptian scientists and engineers work in secret on ballistic missiles and guided weapons. The work is slow and costly, and Western intelligence agencies watch it closely. Israel regards the programme as a direct threat, and the Egyptian leadership sees it as a necessary deterrent.
EGY_1970_the_army_of_the_crossing: After three years of rebuilding, the Egyptian army is no longer the broken host of 1967. It has learned, trained and re-equipped, and it knows exactly what it will do on the day. The soldiers in the sand camps of the west bank wait for the order, certain that the canal will be crossed.
